result:
The last lighthouse keeper on Langaray did not believe in ghosts, but he did believe in the rhythm of things. He knew the exact sound of a foghorn bouncing off a cliff versus the flat, swallowing silence of open water. He knew the way a gale could make the lantern glass hum in a minor key, and how, on the calmest nights, the beam of light seemed to be a solid, golden finger slowly pointing at the sleeping sea.

Tonight, the sea was not sleeping. It was muttering, rolling a low, gravelly discontent under its breath. The barometer in the keeper’s small kitchen had been falling all day, the needle dropping with the slow, inevitable certainty of a diver sinking. He had checked the lens, cleaned the soot from the burner, and reset the clockwork mechanism that turned the great light, ensuring each pulse of brilliance lasted exactly three seconds, followed by a darkness of seven.

He was old enough to remember when the light was powered by oil, and he had to haul the heavy cans up the spiral stairs himself. He remembered his predecessor, a man named O’Shea, who had trained him, who had told him that a lighthouse isn't for the ships. It’s for the keepers. It keeps them from going mad in the dark, giving them a job, a purpose, a single point of focus to push back against the boundless, indifferent ocean.

Now, the automation was complete. A computer, miles away, was supposed to be monitoring everything. A ship was coming tomorrow to take him and the last of his things. He would leave behind the brass fittings, the polished wooden banister, and the logbook that his hand had filled for forty years.

He climbed the stairs one last time, his joints aching more than they had last winter. The light was magnificent. It always was, at night. Up close, it was a huge, crystallized jewel, a monstrous diamond buzzing with power. It was a human-made star, burning in defiance of the dark water and the bruised sky.

He stood there, in the glass room at the top of the world, and listened. The wind began to pick up, a low howl that grew into a shriek before settling into a steady roar. The sea below was a black violence, a chaos of white caps that appeared and vanished like the faces of the drowning. The old keeper put his hand on the cool brass rail. He felt the vibration of the great lamp, a hum that was not of the machinery but of the place itself—its heart, its soul.

The radio crackled. A freighter, the *Mariana*, was twelve miles out and heading into the storm. They confirmed they had him in sight. "Thank you, Keeper," the static-filled voice said. "Light's bright as ever."

He smiled, a small, private smile that no one saw. He didn't tell them that this was the last time. He just replied, "Safe passage."

As the storm broke, hurling rain like handfuls of nails against the glass, he watched his light swing its long, golden arm across the water. He thought about all the nights he had spent at this post, all the cargo ships, the lonely fishermen, the passenger liners full of sleeping people who would never know his name. They saw the flash, they felt the security, and they sailed on.

He wasn't a ghost. He was a man, solid and breathing, standing in a room of glass and light. But as the dawn began to leak into the sky, turning the storm's fury into a grey, tattered mist, he knew that a ghost is simply a place that holds a memory long after its purpose has faded. Tomorrow, this tower would be a thing of the past, a monument to a lonely, violent, beautiful vigilance.

He looked out at the calming sea, and the light, which had been his whole life, still turned. One second of brilliance. Seven seconds of dark. It was a heartbeat. His heartbeat. And he knew, with a profound and quiet certainty, that when he was gone, the light would still be beating, and the sea would still be listening.
